steps.title: Chianti
steps.body: Chianti covers a wide area between Florence and Siena. Chianti Classico is the historic heart, with its black rooster symbol; it's a separate DOCG and must be at least 80% Sangiovese. Since 2014, Gran Selezione sits at the top, from estate grapes with longer ageing. Galestro and alberese soils, rocky marl and limestone, give the best wines.

steps.title: Montalcino and Montepulciano
steps.body: Brunello di Montalcino, south of Siena, is 100% Sangiovese, warmer and drier, with at least five years of ageing, two in oak. Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, from a different hill town, must be at least 70% Sangiovese, called Prugnolo Gentile there. It's not the same as Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, which is a grape and a different region.

options: A wine from the Montepulciano grape, in Abruzzo
steps.explanation: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is made from the Montepulciano grape in Abruzzo. Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is Sangiovese from the Tuscan town.

steps.title: Bolgheri and the coast
steps.body: On Tuscany's coast, Bolgheri became famous with Sassicaia, first sold in 1971, made from Cabernet Sauvignon. Bordeaux grapes thrive in the warm, maritime conditions. Bolgheri DOC now covers these blends, and Sassicaia has its own DOC. Inland, Tignanello blended Sangiovese with Cabernet.
steps.highlight: Bolgheri: Bordeaux grapes on the coast

steps.prompt: Which wines are based on Sangiovese?

steps.title: What you learned
points: Chianti Classico is the historic heart, at least 80% Sangiovese
Brunello is 100% Sangiovese; Vino Nobile at least 70%
Bolgheri grows Bordeaux grapes on the coast
